chat.text: This is a trust product, not a utility — developers have fifty tabs of formatters that phone home, and they'll switch only when the error experience feels like a senior engineer pointing at the exact line instead of a red squiggly line. Ship a 30-second screen recording of the error panel handling a real nested payload with a missing comma, a trailing comma, and a type mismatch so I can write launch copy around what it actually does, not what we hope it does.

This is only worth a polished release if the error panel gives line, column, and a caret under the offending token, not a browser's vague "position 47" message. I demand a differential test suite against JSON.parse on at least 50 malformed and Unicode edge cases, and the UI must highlight the exact failure point before we call it shipped.

Scoring this a 3 on current evidence: a browser-local JSON formatter is trivially reproducible, and "no uploads" is a claim, not a differentiator. Before another line of code, produce a side-by-side benchmark against jsonformatter.org and jq play using a 50MB file and a malformed input with nested quotes and unicode escapes, and prove JSON Forge catches or handles at least one case both competitors objectively miss.

This is a commodity tool drowning in free alternatives — the "local-only" privacy angle won't carry a price tag for developers who already have this in their editor, browser, or a bookmarked site. Prove me wrong by showing a feature that saves a senior engineer 10+ minutes per week that they can't get from VS Code, Chrome DevTools, or a free web tool — then we'll talk pricing.

The "exact error location" spec is the one piece that a single JSON.parse call cannot satisfy reliably, since browser error messages differ wildly across engines. I demand we ship a small hand-rolled tokenizer that reports line, column, and the offending token, and prove it against a malformed-JSON fixture suite before anyone lists this.
